0.1 Compounding and the Time Value of Money

This content was generated by AI. It may contain errors and is not investment advice.

All lessons, questions and reference answers on this site were generated by AI and have not been reviewed by a professional. Their correctness is not guaranteed. If you find an error, please report it with the link at the bottom of the page. The content is for learning only and is not investment advice.

Why money today is worth more

Section titled “Why money today is worth more”

100 dollars today and 100 dollars in one year are not worth the same. There are three reasons:

  • Opportunity cost: money you have today can be invested and grow by next year.
  • Inflation: in one year, the same 100 dollars buys less.
  • Risk: you may not actually receive money that is promised for the future.

So the same amount of money is worth more the earlier you receive it. This is the time value of money. Amounts at different times cannot be added or compared directly; they must first be moved to the same date. Almost every valuation in finance moves future cash flows to today.

Future value and present value

Section titled “Future value and present value”

You deposit 100 dollars today at 10% per year. After one year you have 110 dollars. In the second year, both the principal and the first year’s interest of 10 dollars earn interest, so after two years you have 100×1.12=121100 \times 1.1^2 = 121100×1.12=121 dollars. Interest that itself earns interest is called compound interest. Interest paid only on the principal is called simple interest.

In general, an amount PVPVPV today, compounded at an annual rate rrr for nnn years, grows to

FV=PV (1+r)nFV = PV\,(1+r)^nFV=PV(1+r)n

FVFVFV is the future value. In the other direction, an amount FVFVFV in the future is worth this much today:

PV=FV(1+r)nPV = \frac{FV}{(1+r)^n}PV=(1+r)nFV​

PVPVPV is the present value. The number 1(1+r)n\frac{1}{(1+r)^n}(1+r)n1​ that multiplies FVFVFV is the discount factor, and rrr is also called the discount rate. Moving future money to today is called discounting.

Check C1
The annual interest rate rises from 5% to 6%. Which of these future amounts loses the largest share of its present value?
Money in 1 year is discounted for only one year. Think about whether more years of discounting magnify or shrink the effect of a rate change.
It is affected more than money in 1 year, but another option is discounted for more years.
The discount factor is 1(1+r)n\frac{1}{(1+r)^n}(1+r)n1​. Does the effect of a rate change on it depend on nnn?

Compounding frequency: APR and EAR

Section titled “Compounding frequency: APR and EAR”

A credit card often says “24% per year, interest charged monthly”. The monthly rate is 24%/12=2%24\% / 12 = 2\%24%/12=2%. After one year, 1 dollar becomes

1.0212≈1.26821.02^{12} \approx 1.26821.0212≈1.2682

The actual rate for the year is about 26.82%, more than 24%, because each month’s interest earns interest in the following months. The quoted 24% is the annual percentage rate (APR), and the 26.82% you actually pay is the effective annual rate (EAR). With an annual percentage rate rrr compounded mmm times a year:

EAR=(1+rm)m−1\text{EAR} = \left(1+\frac{r}{m}\right)^m - 1EAR=(1+mr​)m−1

If interest is compounded more and more often, then as m→∞m \to \inftym→∞, (1+rm)m→er\left(1+\frac{r}{m}\right)^m \to e^r(1+mr​)m→er (the proof is left as Exercises Question 7). This is continuous compounding:

FV=PV erTFV = PV\,e^{rT}FV=PVerT

A common estimate is the rule of 72: at an interest rate of xxx%, money doubles in about 72/x72 / x72/x years. For example, at 8% it takes about 9 years. The rule comes from (1+r)n=2(1+r)^n = 2(1+r)n=2, that is,

n=ln⁡2ln⁡(1+r)≈0.693rn = \frac{\ln 2}{\ln(1+r)} \approx \frac{0.693}{r}n=ln(1+r)ln2​≈r0.693​

72 is used instead of 69.3 because it is a little more accurate for common rates and because 72 has many divisors.

Check C2
Two loans both have an annual percentage rate (APR) of 12%; one charges interest monthly and the other yearly. The loan with monthly interest costs more interest over a year.
Think about whether the first month's interest itself earns interest in the following months.

Annuities

Section titled “Annuities”

A series of equal payments at equal intervals is an annuity. Examples are monthly mortgage payments, monthly investments in a fund, and the interest payments of a bond.

What is this series of payments worth today? Amounts at different times cannot be added directly; each payment must be discounted first, and then the results are added. For example, you receive 100 dollars at the end of each year for 3 years, and the discount rate is 10%:

TimeTodayEnd of year 1End of year 2End of year 3
Cash flow (dollars)0100100100
Discounted to today (dollars)90.90982.64575.131
1001.1+1001.12+1001.13≈248.69\frac{100}{1.1} + \frac{100}{1.1^2} + \frac{100}{1.1^3} \approx 248.691.1100​+1.12100​+1.13100​≈248.69

You receive 300 dollars in total, but today it is worth only about 248.69 dollars. The later a payment comes, the more it is discounted.

With a payment CCC at the end of each period, nnn periods and a rate rrr per period, this sum can be written as one formula (the derivation is left as Exercises Question 6):

PV=Cr[1−(1+r)−n]PV = \frac{C}{r}\left[1-(1+r)^{-n}\right]PV=rC​[1−(1+r)−n]

With C=100C = 100C=100, r=0.1r = 0.1r=0.1 and n=3n = 3n=3, it also gives 248.69.

Check C3
The discount rate is 10%. An annuity paying 100 dollars at the end of each year for 20 years has twice the present value of one paying 100 dollars a year for 10 years.
Are the payments of the second 10 years worth as much today as those of the first 10 years?

Perpetuities

Section titled “Perpetuities”

You deposit 1,000 dollars in a bank at 10% per year. At the end of each year you take out the interest of 100 dollars and leave the principal. You can do this forever. So “100 dollars at the end of every year, forever” is worth 1,000 dollars today.

Equal payments at equal intervals that continue forever are a perpetuity. With a payment CCC at the end of each period and a rate rrr per period:

PV=CrPV = \frac{C}{r}PV=rC​
Check C4
The discount rate is 10%. An annuity paying 100 dollars at the end of each year for 50 years is already worth almost as much as a perpetuity paying 100 dollars a year forever (1,000 dollars).
How much are the payments after year 50 worth today?

Future value of an annuity and annuities due

Section titled “Future value of an annuity and annuities due”

You can also ask for the future value of an annuity. You deposit 100 dollars at the end of each year for 3 years at 10%. How much do you have at the end of year 3? The first deposit earns interest for 2 years, the second for 1 year, and the third is just deposited:

100×1.12+100×1.1+100=331100 \times 1.1^2 + 100 \times 1.1 + 100 = 331100×1.12+100×1.1+100=331

In general (the derivation is also left as Exercises Question 6):

FV=C (1+r)n−1rFV = C\,\frac{(1+r)^n - 1}{r}FV=Cr(1+r)n−1​

So far, every payment has been at the end of a period. This is an ordinary annuity, for example mortgage payments and bond interest. If the payments are at the start of each period, as rent usually is, it is an annuity due. Is the present value of an annuity due larger or smaller than that of an ordinary annuity with the same payments, and by how much? Work it out in Exercises Question 6.

Mortgages and regular investing

Section titled “Mortgages and regular investing”

A bank lends you PPP today, and you pay back CCC every month. “Fair” means that at the bank’s interest rate, the present value of all the monthly payments is exactly PPP. Solving the annuity formula for the payment gives

C=P i1−(1+i)−nC = \frac{P\,i}{1-(1+i)^{-n}}C=1−(1+i)−nPi​

Here CCC is the payment each month, so iii is the interest rate per month (the APR divided by 12) and nnn is the number of months.

Example: a loan of 500,000 dollars for 30 years at an APR of 6%. i=0.06/12=0.005i = 0.06 / 12 = 0.005i=0.06/12=0.005 and n=360n = 360n=360:

C=500,000×0.0051−1.005−360≈2,997.75C = \frac{500{,}000 \times 0.005}{1-1.005^{-360}} \approx 2{,}997.75C=1−1.005−360500,000×0.005​≈2,997.75

You pay about 2,997.75 dollars a month, about 1,079,191 dollars over 360 months. About 579,191 dollars of this is interest, which is more than the loan itself.

Regular investing works the other way around. You invest 20,000 dollars at the end of each year for 30 years at 7% per year. With the future value formula for an annuity:

FV=20,000×1.0730−10.07≈1,889,216FV = 20{,}000 \times \frac{1.07^{30} - 1}{0.07} \approx 1{,}889{,}216FV=20,000×0.071.0730−1​≈1,889,216

After 30 years you have about 1.89 million dollars. You put in only 600,000 dollars; the rest comes from compounding.

Growing perpetuities

Section titled “Growing perpetuities”

Some payments continue forever and also grow at a fixed rate each year. For example, you receive rent of 100 dollars at the end of year 1, and the rent rises by 3% every year after that: 100, 103, 106.09, and so on. This is a growing perpetuity. With a payment CCC at the end of period 1, a growth rate ggg and a discount rate rrr:

PV=Cr−gPV = \frac{C}{r-g}PV=r−gC​

Example: 1000.10−0.03≈1,428.57\frac{100}{0.10-0.03} \approx 1{,}428.570.10−0.03100​≈1,428.57. Without growth it would be 1,000 dollars; the growth offsets part of the discounting.

The formula requires g<rg < rg<r; the reason is left as Exercises Question 2. This formula is the basis of the dividend discount model (3.9 Equity Valuation I: Dividend Discount Models).

Check C5
An asset has just paid 5,000 dollars today; from now on it pays at the end of each year, growing 2% a year, forever. When using Cr−g\frac{C}{r-g}r−gC​ to value all the future payments, CCC should be:
Which date's payment is CCC in the formula? Is the 5,000 dollars paid on that date?
The payments grow every year. Is the next payment larger or smaller than today's?
At what rate do the payments grow? Does the discount rate describe how the payments change?

Simple returns and log returns

Section titled “Simple returns and log returns”

When a price changes from P0P_0P0​ to P1P_1P1​, the simple return is

R=P1P0−1R = \frac{P_1}{P_0} - 1R=P0​P1​​−1

Simple returns over several periods must be multiplied, not added:

1+R0→2=(1+R1)(1+R2)1 + R_{0 \to 2} = (1+R_1)(1+R_2)1+R0→2​=(1+R1​)(1+R2​)

Example: the price goes 100 → 80 → 100. The simple returns of the two periods are −20% and +25%. Adding them gives +5%, but the price has not changed. Multiplying gives 0.8×1.25=10.8 \times 1.25 = 10.8×1.25=1, a return of 0 over the two periods, which is correct.

The log return is

ℓ=ln⁡P1P0\ell = \ln\frac{P_1}{P_0}ℓ=lnP0​P1​​

In the example above, the log returns of the two periods are ln⁡0.8≈−0.2231\ln 0.8 \approx -0.2231ln0.8≈−0.2231 and ln⁡1.25≈0.2231\ln 1.25 \approx 0.2231ln1.25≈0.2231, and their sum is exactly 0. Log returns over several periods can simply be added. Why? Explain it in Exercises Question 7.

Assumptions and limits

Section titled “Assumptions and limits”
  • The formulas in this lesson assume a constant interest rate and certain cash flows. Real cash flows are risky, and the risk is reflected in the discount rate (3.10 Equity Valuation II: Discounted Free Cash Flow, 4.4 The Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM)).
  • Nominal cash flows must be discounted with a nominal rate, and real cash flows (after inflation) with a real rate (1.3 Intertemporal Choice).
  • You can check calculations with a spreadsheet or with the Python package numpy-financial (npf.pmt, npf.pv, npf.fv).

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • Amounts at different times must be moved to the same date before they are compared or added: FV=PV(1+r)nFV = PV(1+r)^nFV=PV(1+r)n, PV=FV(1+r)nPV = \frac{FV}{(1+r)^n}PV=(1+r)nFV​.
  • The APR is the quoted rate; the EAR is the rate you actually get after compounding within the year: EAR=(1+rm)m−1\text{EAR} = (1+\frac{r}{m})^m - 1EAR=(1+mr​)m−1. Continuous compounding: FV=PV erTFV = PV\,e^{rT}FV=PVerT.
  • Present value of an annuity: Cr[1−(1+r)−n]\frac{C}{r}[1-(1+r)^{-n}]rC​[1−(1+r)−n]; future value of an annuity: C(1+r)n−1rC\frac{(1+r)^n-1}{r}Cr(1+r)n−1​; perpetuity: Cr\frac{C}{r}rC​; growing perpetuity: Cr−g\frac{C}{r-g}r−gC​.
  • Simple returns over several periods are multiplied; log returns are added.

Exercises

Section titled “Exercises”
Question 1
An advertisement for a savings product says: "10% annual percentage rate, compounded every second. The more often interest is compounded, the more you earn; with frequent enough compounding, the actual return in a year can be as high as you like." Is this right? What does the effective annual rate approach as the compounding frequency grows without limit?
Question 2
Determine whether this statement is true or false, and explain: when g≥rg \ge rg≥r, the formula Cr−g\frac{C}{r-g}r−gC​ shows that the value of a growing perpetuity is infinite.
Question 3
Bank A offers a deposit rate with an APR of 5.0%, compounded daily (365 days a year). Bank B offers an APR of 5.1%, compounded once a year. Which is better? Compute the effective annual rate of each.
Question 4
A loan of 500,000 dollars for 30 years at an annual percentage rate of 6%, repaid monthly. The lesson finds a monthly payment of about 2,997.75 dollars, about 1,079,191 dollars in total over 360 months. A friend says: "The interest is more than the loan itself, so a 30-year mortgage makes you pay more than twice as much. If you have the cash, pay it all at once."
(a) Discounted at 0.5% a month, what are the 360 payments worth today in total? What is wrong with the friend's comparison?
(b) Under what condition is it better to use your cash to repay this loan early?
Question 5
Two funds track the same index. Before fees, both return 7% a year. Their annual fees are 1.00% and 0.05% (the fee is subtracted directly from the annual return). You invest 10,000 dollars once. After 30 years, by what percentage is the future value of the high-fee fund lower than that of the low-fee fund? If you invested every year instead, would the gap caused by fees be larger or smaller? Why?
Question 6 ★
Derive the present value of an ordinary annuity, PV=Cr[1−(1+r)−n]PV = \frac{C}{r}[1-(1+r)^{-n}]PV=rC​[1−(1+r)−n]. Then use it to derive the future value of an annuity and the present value of an annuity due.
